The first line predicts the decisions from the user context. The second line generates the item given the decisions. All decision and SID predictions are trained with cross-entropy in the autoregressive order of Eq. 1, with the ground-truth decisions supplied at their positions (teacher forcing). The resulting retrieval loss is ℒr\mathcal{L}_{r}.

Business Steering. Decoding is a beam search over the decision prefix and the SID codes, so which items are returned depends on how the decision prefixes score against one another. A business objective enters at decoding time by changing that ranking. Decoding proceeds in three steps. First, every valid combination 𝐳\mathbf{z} of the decisions is scored over the cached user context, which gives log⁡P⁡(𝐳∣ℋ)\log P(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathcal{H}) for every decision prefix (Figure 3). Second, a business offset β​ϕ​(𝐳)\beta\,\phi(\mathbf{z}) is added to each of these scores. Third, beam search extends the prefixes into the SID codes, ranking each prefix together with its codes by

log⁡P⁡(𝐳∣ℋ)+β​ϕ​(𝐳)⏟steered decision prefix+∑ℓ=02log⁡P⁡(SIDℓ∣ℋ,𝐳,SID<ℓ).\underbrace{\log P(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathcal{H})+\beta\,\phi(\mathbf{z})}_{\text{steered decision prefix}}\;+\;\sum_{\ell=0}^{2}\log P\!\left(\texttt{SID}_{\ell}\mid\mathcal{H},\mathbf{z},\texttt{SID}_{<\ell}\right). (4)

Here ϕj\phi_{j} assigns an offset to each value of dimension jj. A positive offset on the highest spending level, for instance, steers retrieval toward more valuable orders. ϕ⁡(𝐳)\phi(\mathbf{z}) sums these offsets over the prefix, and the single scalar β\beta sets how strong the whole offset is.

The offset is a soft preference rather than a rule. The first term of Eq. 4 corresponds to the distribution q⁡(𝐳)∝P⁡(𝐳∣ℋ)​eβ​ϕ​(𝐳)q(\mathbf{z})\propto P(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathcal{H})\,e^{\beta\phi(\mathbf{z})}, which is the solution of maxq𝔼q[ϕ(𝐳)]−1βKL(q∥P(⋅∣ℋ))\max_{q}\,\mathbb{E}_{q}[\phi(\mathbf{z})]-\tfrac{1}{\beta}\mathrm{KL}\!\left(q\,\|\,P(\cdot\mid\mathcal{H})\right), the KL-regularized improvement step used in offline reinforcement learning [26]. In words, the offset raises the expected business value of the decisions, a KL penalty keeps them close to what the model learned from the log, and β\beta decides how far they may move. Multi-Game Decision Transformer [19] applies the same idea to a single outcome score. Because ϕ\phi is a sum over dimensions, the exponential factors as eβ​ϕ​(𝐳)=∏jeβ​ϕj​(zj)e^{\beta\phi(\mathbf{z})}=\prod_{j}e^{\beta\phi_{j}(z_{j})}, one factor per objective. Each business objective therefore receives its own offset on its own dimension instead of one global weight.

Three things follow. First, the offset applies only to the decision part of Eq. 4. It changes which decisions win, while the item term P⁡(Item∣ℋ,𝐳)P(\texttt{Item}\mid\mathcal{H},\mathbf{z}) of Eq. 2 is left alone, so under a given decision the model still returns the items it finds most likely. Second, β=0\beta{=}0 gives the model’s own ranking, and a larger β\beta moves further away from it, so the offset adjusts that ranking instead of overriding it. Third, β\beta is set online. Steering toward an objective that the existing dimensions already express therefore needs no retraining. A new objective becomes a new decision dimension, which adds one lightweight decision head to the same model instead of a new retrieval channel with its own model. If the new dimension has no conditional dependence, it is summed into DTp\texttt{DT}^{p} and the decision prefix does not get longer.

Guidance on the Item Side. The business offset decides which decision wins. The same design leaves room for a second control, which would decide how strongly the generated items follow that decision. Classifier-free guidance [16], a technique first developed for diffusion models and later applied to language models [32], can provide it. The idea is to score each SID code twice with the same model, once with the decision prefix and once without it, and to treat the difference between the two scores as the effect of the decision.

To make the second score possible, the decision prefix is replaced with a special null token ∅\varnothing on a small fraction of training samples, so that the model also learns to predict the SID codes when it is told nothing about the decision. At decoding time, each code would then be scored by

log⁡P⁡(SIDℓ∣ℋ,∅,SID<ℓ)+w⁡[log⁡P⁡(SIDℓ∣ℋ,𝐳,SID<ℓ)−log⁡P⁡(SIDℓ∣ℋ,∅,SID<ℓ)].\log P(\texttt{SID}_{\ell}\mid\mathcal{H},\varnothing,\texttt{SID}_{<\ell})+w\,\big[\log P(\texttt{SID}_{\ell}\mid\mathcal{H},\mathbf{z},\texttt{SID}_{<\ell})-\log P(\texttt{SID}_{\ell}\mid\mathcal{H},\varnothing,\texttt{SID}_{<\ell})\big]. (5)

The bracket measures how much knowing the decision 𝐳\mathbf{z} changes the score of a code, and the weight ww scales that change. With w=1w{=}1 the score equals the ordinary item term of Eq. 4. With w>1w{>}1 the effect of the decision is amplified, so the retrieved items follow it more closely. With w<1w{<}1 the effect is weakened, and with w=0w{=}0 the decision is ignored. Because both scores come from the same model, their difference is largely unaffected by how well either score is calibrated. Computing the second score requires a second pass of the decoder, but both passes read the same cached user context and differ only at the prefix and SID positions, so the extra work is confined to the beam search. Steering would then have two online parameters. The offset β\beta decides which decision is made, and the weight ww decides how closely the items follow it. The interventions of §7.4 suggest that the decoder responds to its prefix strongly enough for ww to have an effect. This extension is not yet deployed, and we leave its evaluation to future work.

4.2.2 Discriminative Ranking Tasks

Pre-rank. Pre-rank scores every candidate that retrieval returns, so its per-candidate budget is the tightest in the cascade, and it can neither read the full non-sequential feature set nor afford many tokens for each candidate. We therefore restrict pre-rank to a lightweight feature subset 𝒩​𝒮p⊂𝒩​𝒮f\mathcal{NS}_{p}\subset\mathcal{NS}_{f} and let its tokenizer compress the whole subset into a single candidate token. This token attends to the shared user context under the stage visibility mask. The pre-rank heads read out its resulting state and predict the pre-rank target set 𝒯p\mathcal{T}_{p} of CTR and CVR, each optimized by a binary cross-entropy loss ℒp\mathcal{L}_{p},

ℒp=−∑t∈𝒯p[yptlogy^pt+(1−ypt)log(1−y^pt)],\mathcal{L}_{p}=-\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{p}}\left[y_{p}^{t}\log\hat{y}_{p}^{t}+(1-y_{p}^{t})\log(1-\hat{y}_{p}^{t})\right], (6)

where ypt∈{0,1}y_{p}^{t}\in\{0,1\} and y^pt\hat{y}_{p}^{t} denote the label and the predicted probability of target tt, respectively.

Fine-rank. Fine-rank scores only the candidates that survive pre-rank and determines the final order. Its main constraint therefore moves from per-candidate throughput to ranking fidelity, and pooling its rich candidate features into one token would erase the feature heterogeneity that this fidelity depends on. Following OneTrans [53], we let fine-rank consume the full non-sequential set 𝒩​𝒮f\mathcal{NS}_{f} and keep it as multiple tokens rather than the single token that pre-rank uses. These tokens attend to the shared user context under the same stage visibility mask, and their resulting states are read out by the fine-rank heads, which predict the fine-rank targets. Unlike pre-rank, fine-rank predicts many more objectives; we focus on the core ones, CTR and CVR, denoted 𝒯f\mathcal{T}_{f}, again with a binary cross-entropy loss ℒf\mathcal{L}_{f},

ℒf=−∑t∈𝒯f[yftlogy^ft+(1−yft)log(1−y^ft)],\mathcal{L}_{f}=-\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{f}}\left[y_{f}^{t}\log\hat{y}_{f}^{t}+(1-y_{f}^{t})\log(1-\hat{y}_{f}^{t})\right], (7)

where yfty_{f}^{t} and y^ft\hat{y}_{f}^{t} are the label and the predicted probability of target tt as in Eq. 6.

Knowledge Distillation. Sharing the user context gives pre-rank and fine-rank a common representation, but each stage still learns its own scoring function, and the two can order the same candidates differently. This is problematic, as a candidate that pre-rank discards can never be recovered by fine-rank, so every disagreement between the two stages permanently removes items that fine-rank would have ranked at the top. To address this, we adopt knowledge distillation [15] between the two ranking stages, with the fine-rank task as the teacher and the pre-rank task as the student. The stage with the richer candidate features thus supervises the ordering produced by the cheaper one. We follow the mean-centering step of logit standardization [41] but replace the standard deviation by a fixed temperature τ\tau. For each pre-rank target t∈𝒯pt\in\mathcal{T}_{p}, the teacher logit otTo^{T}_{t} and the student logit otSo^{S}_{t} are centered by their respective means μtT\mu^{T}_{t} and μtS\mu^{S}_{t}, and the resulting student probability is trained against the teacher probability with a binary cross-entropy loss ℒk​d\mathcal{L}_{kd} summed over the targets,

pTt=σ(otT−μtTτ),pSt=σ(otS−μtSτ),ℒk​d=−∑t∈𝒯p[pTtlogpSt+(1−pTt)log(1−pSt)],\begin{gathered}p^{T}_{t}=\sigma\!\left(\frac{o^{T}_{t}-\mu^{T}_{t}}{\tau}\right),\qquad p^{S}_{t}=\sigma\!\left(\frac{o^{S}_{t}-\mu^{S}_{t}}{\tau}\right),\\ \mathcal{L}_{kd}=-\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{p}}\Big[\,p^{T}_{t}\log p^{S}_{t}+(1-p^{T}_{t})\log(1-p^{S}_{t})\Big],\end{gathered} (8)

where σ\sigma is the sigmoid function. To prevent the distillation loss from affecting the teacher, we detach the teacher logit, allowing it to be shaped only by the fine-rank objective while the alignment moves the student alone. Because of the one-model design of OneTrans-V2, this distillation requires neither a separately trained teacher nor an offline distillation stage. We optimize ℒk​d\mathcal{L}_{kd} together with the task losses in the same backward pass, so the student keeps improving as the teacher itself grows stronger.

4.2.3 Overall Objective

OneTrans-V2 is optimized via ℒ\mathcal{L}, a weighted sum of the three task objectives and the distillation loss ℒk​d\mathcal{L}_{kd},

ℒ=λr​ℒr+λp​ℒp+λf​ℒf+λk​d​ℒk​d,\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{r}\mathcal{L}_{r}+\lambda_{p}\mathcal{L}_{p}+\lambda_{f}\mathcal{L}_{f}+\lambda_{kd}\mathcal{L}_{kd}, (9)

where λr\lambda_{r}, λp\lambda_{p}, λf\lambda_{f}, and λk​d\lambda_{kd} control the relative contributions of the four objectives.

4.3 Scaling and Stabilization

Scaling OneTrans-V2 requires increasing model capacity while bounding activated computation and maintaining effective attention and stable optimization. To this end, we combine parameter-efficient scaling, stabilization, and optimization techniques, and revisit which input designs remain beneficial at scale.

TransBlock Design. Figure 2(b) expands the internal structure of a TransBlock. Each block follows the pre-norm layout, in which an RMSNorm [52] precedes the attention and FFN sub-layers and a residual connection follows each. The branch output is scaled by a residual multiplier γ=1/2​N\gamma=1/\sqrt{2N} for NN blocks, so the residual stream stays bounded as the model deepens. In the attention sub-layer, queries and keys are RMS-normalized per head (QKNorm [14]), and gated attention [30] modulates the attention output before the output projection. The FFN sub-layer is a sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE), which routes each token to a small subset of experts. This grows the parameter count while keeping the activated compute per token roughly constant. Algorithm 1 summarizes the forward pass of a block, and we detail each component below.

Grouped-Query Attention. On the attention side, we adopt grouped-query attention (GQA) [1]. The query heads are partitioned into groups, and every group shares a single key/value head, so a layer keeps far fewer key/value heads than query heads. The saving matters because the key/value cache of the shared behavior sequence is computed once and then read by the stage-specific tokens of all three tasks. During retrieval it is further broadcast across the beams of the decoder. Its size therefore sets both the memory footprint and the memory traffic of every cross-attention step. GQA shrinks this cache in proportion to the group size without loss in quality (§7.6). Only the number of key/value heads and the head dimension must agree between the stage-specific tokens and the shared behavior sequence. The two are therefore free to use different numbers of query heads over the same cached keys and values.

Sparse MoE. Following DeepSeekMoE [5], the FFN in OneTrans-V2 is a sparse MoE built from fine-grained experts, SwiGLU networks [35] with a narrow intermediate width. One shared expert is always active, and the rest form a set of routed experts. For each input, a lightweight router produces one score per routed expert, and a fixed number of the highest-scoring routed experts are selected. Their scores are renormalized to sum to one and multiplied by a fixed routed-expert scaling factor. The sub-layer output is the shared expert’s output plus the weighted sum of the selected routed experts. Inspired by DeepSeek-V3 [7], we adopt a sigmoid router rather than a softmax one. A softmax couples the experts, since raising the score of one necessarily lowers all the others. This pushes the router toward winner-take-all routing and ties the scale of every score to the total number of experts. A sigmoid scores each expert’s relevance to the input independently and on a fixed scale. Several experts can then be judged relevant at once, and the scores remain comparable as experts are added, which eases training at larger expert counts.

Gated Attention. We adopt gated attention [30], which applies a head-specific, input-dependent sigmoid gate to the attention output. The gate logits are produced from the normalized attention input by an extra slice of the fused QKVG projection. The softmax-weighted values of every attention head are multiplied element-wise by the sigmoid of these gate logits before the output projection. The gate therefore controls what each head writes back to the residual stream rather than the attention distribution itself. Sitting between the value and output projections, it adds a non-linearity that keeps the two from collapsing into a single linear map. It also yields input-dependent sparsity, so a head that is uninformative for the current token can be switched off instead of placing its attention mass on a sink position. This suppresses attention sinks and massive activations and improves training stability.

Stabilization Techniques. As the model grows in width and depth, training becomes harder. The scales of the activations, gradients, and per-step weight updates all drift with model size, so a configuration that is stable at one size can diverge at the next. Each scaling step would then call for a fresh hyperparameter search, at a scale where every trial is expensive. We therefore parameterize the backbone so that its training dynamics stay invariant as the model grows, following the maximal update parameterization (μ\muP) [48] for width and Depth-μ\muP [49] for depth. Both rest on one principle. Scaling changes how many terms each layer sums. The initialization, the multipliers, and the learning rate must therefore be chosen together. The goal is that every hidden activation and its per-step change stay at a scale that neither grows nor vanishes with model size, which we write as Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1). For width, consider a hidden layer W​𝐱W\mathbf{x} with input 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and weight matrix WW, where dd is the width. Fan-in initialization, i.e., entries of WW with variance 1/d1/d, already keeps W​𝐱W\mathbf{x} at Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1), since its dd terms are uncorrelated at initialization. An Adam step with learning rate η\eta, however, changes every entry of WW by roughly η\eta. The resulting change Δ​W​𝐱\Delta W\,\mathbf{x} sums dd terms that are correlated with 𝐱\mathbf{x}, so it grows as Θ⁡(η​d)\Theta(\eta d). μ\muP cancels this growth by scaling the Adam learning rate of every hidden weight by 1/d1/d. For depth, let NN be the number of blocks, each adding an attention branch and an FFN branch to the residual stream. The stream sums 2​N2N branch outputs that are nearly uncorrelated at initialization, so a 1/2​N1/\sqrt{2N} residual multiplier keeps the forward signal at Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1). The updates of different branches, however, are correlated through the shared loss and add up rather than cancel, so the total update grows as NN. The residual multiplier already cancels one factor of N\sqrt{N} of this growth, and under Adam the learning rate must be scaled by 1/N1/\sqrt{N} to cancel the other. Table 1 lists the resulting rules for the hidden layers relative to a base model of width d0d_{0} and depth N0N_{0}, in terms of the width multiplier md=d/d0m_{d}=d/d_{0} and the depth multiplier mN=N/N0m_{N}=N/N_{0}.

Two further quantities drift during training rather than with model size. The attention logits grow with the norms of the query and key projections, so we apply QKNorm [14] to the queries and keys. This holds the logits in a fixed range and keeps the softmax from collapsing onto a single position. The weight norms themselves grow under Adam, and the effective learning rate shrinks with them. We therefore optimize the dense parameters with AdamW, whose decoupled weight decay [21] holds the norms at a stable level.

Multimodal Embedding. Capacity also changes how an item’s multimodal embedding should enter the model. The established practice, SimTier [36], does not feed the multimodal embedding itself. For every behavior sequence, it computes the cosine similarity between the candidate and each item of that sequence, summarizes those scores into a histogram, and feeds the histogram to the model as a dense feature. OneTrans-V2 instead feeds the multimodal embedding directly, as side information on every behavior item and on the candidate. This choice is beneficial only with sufficient capacity, as §7.8 shows.

4.4 Sequence-Native Training

A larger backbone makes every training step more expensive, and the largest part of that cost is encoding the long behavior sequence. Conventional recommendation training pays this cost many times over, because each stage builds its own training samples, one per exposure or one per request, and every sample carries its own copy of the sequence. A user with a hundred exposures therefore has that sequence copied and encoded up to a hundred times. Methods such as RLB [11] and MTGR [13] reduce this redundancy by grouping exposures around a shared user context. SNT extends this reuse across the cascade. The sequence is encoded once, and every exposure reads from that encoding, whichever request and whichever stage it comes from.

Two properties make this possible. First, the behavior sequence is append-only and is encoded with causal attention [53]. The hidden state at each position therefore summarizes only the behaviors up to that position, and the encoding of the whole sequence contains the encoding of every earlier prefix unchanged. Second, each exposure keeps its own request identity, timestamp, task identity, stage-specific features, and labels, but it no longer carries a copy of the behavior sequence. In the model, an exposure appears as its stage-specific tokens attached to the shared encoding under the stage visibility mask, and it reads only the prefix up to its request time, as the next paragraph describes. To make this sharing work in practice, SNT also changes how the training samples are grouped. Exposures are grouped by user, so that the exposures of one user within a time window (a user window) are stored and read together with one copy of that user’s behavior sequence. The length of that window is a configuration choice (§7.9).

What Each Exposure Sees. Formally, exposure ee is anchored at the position aea_{e} of the last behavior in 𝒮u\mathcal{S}_{u} that had arrived by its request time (§4.1). Under the stage visibility mask it attends only to the prefix up to aea_{e}. Exposures from the same request share one anchor. Each exposure therefore sees exactly what the model saw online at that request, even though the sequence was encoded once for all of them. We call this the causal view of an exposure, and Figure 4 illustrates it for two requests.

The views stay valid as the sequence grows because it is append-only. Let 𝒮u(n)\mathcal{S}_{u}^{(n)} denote the sequence seen by the nn-th request. The sequence seen by the next request is

𝒮u(n+1)=𝒮u(n)|Δ​𝒮u(n+1),\mathcal{S}_{u}^{(n+1)}=\mathcal{S}_{u}^{(n)}\,\|\,\Delta\mathcal{S}_{u}^{(n+1)}, (10)

where ∥\| denotes concatenation and Δ​𝒮u(n+1)\Delta\mathcal{S}_{u}^{(n+1)} contains the behaviors that arrive between the two requests. Because new behaviors are appended and never inserted into an earlier prefix, the causal states and anchors defined on 𝒮u(n)\mathcal{S}_{u}^{(n)} remain valid in 𝒮u(n+1)\mathcal{S}_{u}^{(n+1)}.

Request-Relative Time Encoding. The anchor decides which behaviors an exposure can see, but not how old they are. A behavior from yesterday matters differently to a request made today than to one made a month later. Yet both requests read the same encoded sequence. We therefore make the attention between stage-specific tokens and the behavior sequence depend on the time difference between the request and the behavior. We use a timestamp-based variant [24] of rotary position encoding [38]. The query of an exposure at request time tet_{e} is rotated by tet_{e}, and the key of a behavior at event time tit_{i} is rotated by tit_{i}. For the temporal channels, the attention term then satisfies

(R⁡(te)​𝐪etime)⊤​(R⁡(ti)​𝐤itime)=(𝐪etime)⊤​R​(ti−te)​𝐤itime,\left(R(t_{e})\mathbf{q}_{e}^{\mathrm{time}}\right)^{\top}\left(R(t_{i})\mathbf{k}_{i}^{\mathrm{time}}\right)=(\mathbf{q}_{e}^{\mathrm{time}})^{\top}R(t_{i}-t_{e})\mathbf{k}_{i}^{\mathrm{time}}, (11)

where R⁡(t)R(t) denotes the rotary transformation for timestamp tt. The term depends only on ti−tet_{i}-t_{e}, not on where the behavior sits in the sequence. Tokens of the same exposure share one request time, so their relative rotation cancels. Behavior self-attention is left unchanged. We use multiple fixed temporal periods to capture both short- and long-term dynamics. The rotation of a key depends only on the behavior’s own timestamp. The rotated keys are therefore computed once and reused by every request and stage, and each exposure contributes only its own query and anchor.

Compared with exposure-centric samples, SNT yields a 4.4×4.4\times training speedup under the same hardware budget (§7.9).

5 Serving and System Optimization

5.1 Serving Pipeline

Although OneTrans-V2 is jointly trained as one Transformer, serving still follows the original retrieval →\to pre-rank →\to fine-rank cascade, with each stage executing only its own candidate-side computation.

Shared User Context. For an online request from user uu, the behavior sequence 𝒮u\mathcal{S}_{u} is first processed by the shared causal Transformer to produce a reusable user-context cache CuC_{u}. The same CuC_{u} is then consumed by retrieval, pre-rank, and fine-rank, so the long behavior sequence is encoded once per request rather than once per stage. Retrieval consumes CuC_{u} together with the retrieval-specific features 𝒩​𝒮r\mathcal{NS}_{r} and performs DCGR decoding, applying the business offset of §4.2.1 to the prefix scores, followed by beam search over the SID hierarchy. Pre-rank and fine-rank are non-autoregressive candidate-scoring passes over the same CuC_{u}. Pre-rank uses the lightweight feature set 𝒩​𝒮p\mathcal{NS}_{p} to score the retrieved candidates, while fine-rank applies the richer 𝒩​𝒮f\mathcal{NS}_{f} only to the surviving candidates. The candidate set therefore continues to shrink through the cascade even though the user context is shared.

5.2 Decoding and Kernel Optimization

Retrieval Decoding Optimization. Retrieval first generates the decision prefix and then decodes the SID codes with beam search. Both are decoded step by step, so their latency is set by the number of sequential steps and the work per step. We reduce the former for the prefix and the latter for SID decoding. For the decision prefix, every dimension has a small vocabulary. There are three values for the purchase level zo​cz_{oc}, two for the supply type za​dz_{ad}, and a few each for the discovery level zd​i​s​cz_{disc} and the spending level za​o​vz_{aov}. Their product is small enough to score in a single forward pass. Rather than decoding the parallel and chained positions one after another, we therefore enumerate all valid combinations of 𝐳\mathbf{z} in Eq. 3 and score them in one forward pass over the cached user context. This collapses the prefix from multiple sequential steps to a single scoring step, which is where the business offset acts. For SID decoding, write kk for the beam width and KK for the number of items the search finally returns to pre-rank. We replace the global top-kk over all beam–token pairs with a two-stage top-kk, which first retains the kk best extensions of each beam and then selects the global top-kk among them. This yields exactly the same top-kk set. The intermediate candidate pool shrinks from the beam width times the vocabulary size to kk per beam, which cuts the work per step accordingly.

Kernel Fusion. Beyond the decoding changes above, a set of kernel-level optimizations raises the model FLOPs utilization (MFU) of every forward pass in both training and serving. On modern GPUs, utilization is governed by the size and number of GEMMs and by the memory traffic of the element-wise operations between them. We therefore make the GEMMs larger and fewer and fuse whatever lies in between. The attention between the stage-specific tokens and the shared behavior sequence runs on a FlashAttention-style kernel [6] whose built-in stage visibility mask covers all candidates of a user in one call, without padding or materializing the attention matrix. Within a TransBlock, the query, key, value, and gate projections are issued as one bias-free general matrix multiplication (GEMM) whose output is consumed in place. QKNorm is applied by an RMSNorm kernel that addresses the query and key slices through offsets rather than copies. The gate and up projections of SwiGLU are likewise merged into one GEMM. Each fused kernel is written to exploit the efficient instructions of modern GPUs. For example, the RMSNorm kernel guarantees that every token’s hidden vector starts at a 16-byte-aligned address, so the compiler can emit 128-bit vectorized loads that fetch eight 16-bit values per instruction.

Low-Precision Serving. Unlike LLMs, recommendation models consume many floating-point features whose value ranges and precision must be preserved, so serving runs in FP16 by default. The Transformer backbone itself is more tolerant, since the RMSNorm before every sub-layer and on the queries and keys keeps its activations on a bounded scale. We therefore push the SwiGLU GEMMs, which account for about two thirds of the FLOPs of a TransBlock, further down to FP8. Serving also admits one fusion that training cannot. With no backward pass that needs the intermediate activations, the merged gate-and-up GEMM, the down GEMM, and the scaled residual update of SwiGLU run as a single kernel.

6 Experimental Results

6.1 Experimental Setup

Dataset. We evaluate OneTrans-V2 offline on production logs from a large-scale industrial recommendation system. The logs are collected with the same logging, feature-snapshot, and labeling pipeline as OneTrans [53] but over a different time window, so absolute numbers are not comparable with those reported there. The production logs are kept in chronological order, and every feature is recorded at exposure time to avoid temporal leakage and to keep offline evaluation consistent with online serving. Labels such as clicks and orders are accumulated over the fixed windows used in production. All logs are collected in compliance with strict privacy policies, with personally identifiable information anonymized and hashed.

Tasks and Metrics. We evaluate all three stages. Retrieval is generative and decodes SID codes with beam search rather than scoring a fixed candidate set. Following UniSGR [40], we measure it with HitRate@MM (HR@MM), the fraction of requests whose ground-truth item has its SID among the top-MM SIDs that beam search returns, and report M=1M{=}1 and M=10M{=}10. Pre-rank and fine-rank score a given candidate set, and we report AUC and UAUC (exposure-weighted user-level AUC) for both CTR and CVR. Both stages and their baselines are trained and evaluated on the same exposures and labels, without unexposed candidates or sampled negatives.

Following the next-batch protocol of OneTrans [53], we stream the data chronologically and score each mini-batch before it updates the model, so no prediction is made on data the model has already trained on. Metrics are computed daily and macro-averaged over the evaluation period. We also report serving GFLOPs, the floating-point cost that a model spends on one request under the deployed configuration, summed over the stages it serves.11 1 OneTrans [53] reported training FLOPs. Here we report serving FLOPs instead, since the cost of serving a request is what bounds the QPS and latency of the deployed cascade. This is the cost actually executed after the optimizations described in OneTrans. For example, the candidates that a stage scores for a request share one encoding of the behavior sequence, so the encoding is counted once rather than once per candidate.

Implementation. We evaluate OneTrans-V2 (§4) at two scales. Our default, OneTrans-V2L (L for large), stacks the TransBlocks of §4.3 and costs 662662 GFLOPs per request. OneTrans-V2S (S for small) is a lighter variant of the same design that costs 239239 GFLOPs per request, about 36%36\% of OneTrans-V2L. For the retrieval task, we quantize each item into three SID codes with a codebook of 81928192 entries per level. The decision prefix covers four dimensions (zo​cz_{oc}, zd​i​s​cz_{disc}, za​dz_{ad}, za​o​vz_{aov}) laid out over two token positions.

During training, we use a dual-optimizer strategy. Sparse embeddings are optimized with AdaGrad [8], with a learning rate of 0.10.1 and an initial accumulator value of 1.01.0. Dense parameters are optimized with AdamW [21]22 2 Weight decay follows the convention of modern LLM training, i.e., a decoupled shrinkage W←W−η​ω​WW\leftarrow W-\eta\omega W with weight decay coefficient ω\omega, scaled by the learning rate η\eta rather than a learning-rate-independent step W←W−ω​WW\leftarrow W-\omega W, as in TensorFlow’s legacy AdamW. (Adam β1=0\beta_{1}{=}0, β2=0.99999\beta_{2}{=}0.99999, ϵ=10−5\epsilon{=}10^{-5}, weight decay 0.010.01). With β1=0\beta_{1}{=}0 this optimizer carries no momentum and reduces to RMSProp with bias correction of the second moment and decoupled weight decay. We keep the name AdamW for the implementation it uses. Beyond the stabilization techniques of §4.3, we use global gradient-norm clipping [25] for both dense and sparse layers, and we train in BF16 with a per-GPU batch size of 20482048 on 16 GPUs. In the training objective (Eq. 9), the retrieval, pre-rank, and fine-rank losses carry weights λr=0.1\lambda_{r}{=}0.1, λp=1\lambda_{p}{=}1, and λf=1\lambda_{f}{=}1, and the distillation loss carries λk​d=1\lambda_{kd}{=}1 at a temperature of τ=0.5\tau{=}0.5. The centering means of Eq. 8 are maintained as exponential moving averages over training batches with momentum 0.99990.9999.

Baselines. We compare OneTrans-V2 against the following baselines, all trained with the same features:

  • •

    OneTrans-GR is our deployed generative retrieval (GR) model, a standalone SID-only model without the decision prefix. It represents each item by a three-level SID (§4.2.1) and autoregressively decodes its codes with a Transformer decoder. It is the most recently developed GR model in our system, built after OneTrans [53] and at a much larger scale. This makes it a strong baseline rather than a lightly tuned reference model.

  • •

    OneTrans-Lite is our deployed pre-rank model, a compact variant of OneTrans that fits the tighter compute budget of pre-rank.

  • •

    OneTrans [53] is our deployed fine-rank model, which jointly models a user’s behavior sequences and non-sequential features within a single Transformer (§3).

  • •

    UniSGR [40] and UniPinRec [20] are two recent frameworks that unify generative retrieval with a downstream ranking component. In our reproduction, we map UniPinRec’s lightweight ranking task to pre-rank and UniSGR’s multi-objective ranking task to fine-rank, and we decode UniSGR’s retrieval following its original implementation, in which the task token is set externally rather than predicted from the behavior sequence. Since each couples only two stages, we compare each model on the stages represented by this mapping. UniPinRec’s retrieval is the one exception, as it is not generative but retrieves by nearest-neighbor search over item embeddings, and we therefore do not compare it against the SID-based generative retrieval models reported here.

6.2 Offline Performance

Table 2 summarizes the performance of OneTrans-V2 and the corresponding baselines across the three stages. The existing cascade, i.e., OneTrans-GR for retrieval, OneTrans-Lite for pre-rank, and OneTrans for fine-rank, together costs 275275 GFLOPs per request. This is the reference for the comparisons below.

OneTrans-V2S serves all three stages at 239239 GFLOPs, slightly under that reference, yet surpasses each of the three baselines on the stage it serves, by +21.10%+21.10\% on retrieval HR@1 and +2.17%+2.17\% on fine-rank CVR UAUC, for example. OneTrans-V2L spends 2.4×2.4\times as much as the cascade and turns the extra compute into larger gains on all ten metrics. It lifts retrieval HR@1 by 69.36%69.36\% over OneTrans-GR, pre-rank CTR UAUC by 4.65%4.65\% and CVR UAUC by 3.14%3.14\% over OneTrans-Lite, and fine-rank CTR UAUC by 2.31%2.31\% and CVR UAUC by 3.42%3.42\% over OneTrans. Both variants also surpass UniPinRec and UniSGR, two recent models that unify multiple stages, on every stage they cover. The part of these gains that comes from joint training alone, under matched architecture and parameter budget, is isolated in §7.1.

6.3 Online A/B Performance

We assess the business impact of OneTrans-V2 with online A/B tests in a large-scale industrial recommendation system. The control group is served by the existing cascade of OneTrans-GR, OneTrans-Lite, and OneTrans. In the treatment group, a single OneTrans-V2L, served with the stack of §5.2, replaces all three. Traffic is split at the user level with hashing-based randomization, with 50%50\% of traffic assigned to each group.

OneTrans-V2 lifts GMV per user by 9.74%9.74\% over the control group. It also raises user active days by 0.25%0.25\%, so the items it recommends bring users back more often. These gains are measured against a strong cascade of three separately trained and separately served models, and they show the potential of cascade-level unification.

OneTrans-V2 also serves more efficiently. We define QPS as the number of requests completed per second through all three stages. Under the same hardware budget, the treatment group is served at 3.2×3.2\times the QPS of the control group, even though OneTrans-V2 executes more FLOPs per request. The higher QPS comes from the serving stack and from encoding the behavior sequence once per request rather than once per stage, and §7.9 quantifies both.

7 Analysis

In this section, we analyze what each component of OneTrans-V2 contributes. Unless noted otherwise, ranking results are reported on CTR, and every improvement represents a relative change against the corresponding reference configuration instead of an absolute difference in AUC or UAUC.

7.1 Effect of Joint Training

We analyze whether training the three tasks jointly outperforms training each of them separately. Throughout this subsection, the joint model and its separately trained counterparts share the same architecture, parameter budget, training data, and training objective, with the loss weights of §6.1 unchanged. This includes the distillation loss of §4.2.2, which the separately trained pre-rank receives from the separately trained fine-rank. Any gain therefore reflects joint training rather than added capacity or distillation. We first analyze merging pre-rank with fine-rank, and then analyze merging all three stages together.

Combining Pre-rank and Fine-rank. We start with the two ranking tasks, letting their tokens read one shared user context and optimizing them together. Table 3 shows that both tasks improve over their separately trained counterparts. Pre-rank gains +0.09%+0.09\% CTR AUC and +0.17%+0.17\% CTR UAUC, and fine-rank gains +0.12%+0.12\% CTR AUC and +0.21%+0.21\% CTR UAUC. The two tasks therefore reinforce each other rather than compete.

Combining All Three Stages. We then add the retrieval task and train all three together, and Figure 5 compares every task against its separately trained counterpart. With the retrieval gradient into the shared user context stopped, the retrieval task33 3 In this experiment the retrieval task of the joint model and its separately trained counterpart share the same backbone and compute budget as OneTrans-GR, so that the comparison isolates joint training from capacity. reuses the shared user context already shaped by the ranking tasks and gains +7.63%+7.63\% on HR@1. Pre-rank and fine-rank gain +0.19%+0.19\% and +0.21%+0.21\% CTR UAUC.44 4 These differ slightly from Table 3 because the embedding tables remain shared, so the retrieval task still has a small effect on pre-rank and fine-rank even with its gradient into the shared user context stopped. We then let the retrieval gradient flow into the shared user context, so that its next-token prediction objective also shapes the user context the ranking tasks read. This roughly doubles the retrieval task’s gain to +15.44%+15.44\% and raises pre-rank and fine-rank to +0.28%+0.28\% and +0.31%+0.31\% CTR UAUC. Unifying all three tasks therefore improves every task over training them separately, with the retrieval objective further strengthening the shared user context for ranking.

7.2 Distillation and Consistency between the Ranking Stages

Knowledge Distillation. The previous subsection shows that joint training helps all three tasks. For the two ranking tasks, OneTrans-V2 adds a second mechanism, the knowledge distillation of §4.2.2, an extra loss ℒk​d\mathcal{L}_{kd} in which the fine-rank logits supervise the pre-rank ones. Figure 6(a) shows what this loss contributes. This ablation is orthogonal to the joint-training comparison, where both settings keep ℒk​d\mathcal{L}_{kd}; here the joint model drops it. Removing ℒk​d\mathcal{L}_{kd} from OneTrans-V2 while holding the architecture, data, and every other hyperparameter fixed costs pre-rank 0.55%0.55\% CTR AUC and 0.97%0.97\% CTR UAUC. This shows how much distillation contributes to closing the gap between pre-rank and fine-rank. Fine-rank itself moves by at most 0.04%0.04\%, as the detached teacher logit intends, so the student’s gain is not paid for by the teacher.

Cross-Stage Consistency. We further analyze how consistently pre-rank and fine-rank order the same candidates online. Both the shared user context and the distillation loss pull the two stages together, and Figure 6(b) measures their combined effect with two metrics, the inversion rate and top-10 and top-50 coverage. The inversion rate is the fraction of item pairs that the two tasks order differently, and top-10 coverage is the fraction of pre-rank’s top 10 that also appears in fine-rank’s top 10, and likewise for top-50. Both are computed over the candidates that pre-rank forwards to fine-rank. Compared with the separately trained pre-rank and fine-rank of §7.1, OneTrans-V2 reduces the inversion rate by 6.7%6.7\% and raises top-10 and top-50 coverage by 31.4%31.4\% and 13.5%13.5\%, all as relative changes. The two ranking stages therefore disagree less often. More importantly, pre-rank forwards far more of fine-rank’s top candidates, so fewer of the items that fine-rank would place at the top are discarded before fine-rank ever sees them.

7.3 Objective Coverage of DCGR

As described in §1, retrieval in our production system is split into specialized channels for different business objectives. The main channel, served by OneTrans-GR, targets clicks and orders, the discovery channel promotes categories new to the user, and the advertising channel retrieves sponsored items. DCGR represents these objectives within a single model through corresponding decision dimensions. Specifically, the purchase level zo​cz_{oc} captures the main channel’s click-and-order objective, the discovery level zd​i​s​cz_{disc} captures the discovery objective, and the supply type za​dz_{ad} distinguishes organic from sponsored items for advertising. This moves the three objectives from separate retrieval channels into one shared decision space. We next ask whether a single DCGR can still cover what each specialized channel was built to provide.

We test this with an online retrieval-stage A/B test, with traffic split equally at the user level. In the treatment group, OneTrans-V2’s retrieval task, i.e., DCGR, replaces OneTrans-GR in the main channel, and the discovery and advertising channels are switched off, so the three channels are unified by a single model. The control group keeps all three channels as deployed. Because the three channels serve different purposes, we evaluate each objective with its native metric, namely GMV for the main objective, the number of categories new to the user per reached user for discovery, and GMV per thousand exposures (GPM) on sponsored items for advertising.

Figure 7 shows that DCGR covers all three objectives within one model. It produces 1.5×1.5\times the GMV of the control group’s main channel, reaches 2.2×2.2\times as many categories new to the user per reached user as the discovery channel, and achieves 2.1×2.1\times the sponsored-item GPM of the advertising channel. Thus, a single DCGR matches or exceeds the specialized channel on the metric native to each objective.

Main Channel Analysis. The 1.5×1.5\times GMV gain on the main objective comes primarily from broader exposure rather than higher value per exposure. Table 4(a) shows that DCGR increases exposures by 69.3%69.3\% and clicks by 74.6%74.6\% over the control group’s main channel. Part of that volume is what the discovery and advertising channels served in the control group, since DCGR now serves it as well. Its per-exposure conversion is lower. Specifically, orders per thousand exposures decrease by 34.0%34.0\%, and GMV per thousand exposures by 13.0%13.0\%. The larger exposure volume nevertheless more than offsets these declines, increasing total orders by 11.4%11.4\% and total GMV by 48.0%48.0\%. CTR per exposure also increases by 3.2%3.2\%. The average price of an exposed item decreases by 4.4%4.4\%, indicating that the additional exposures are concentrated more heavily on lower-priced items.

These measurements compare one channel against another rather than one system against another. DCGR serves in the treatment group the exposures that all three channels served in the control group, so its margin over the main channel alone is not the value it adds to the system. Figure 7 therefore measures which objectives DCGR can cover, not how much it adds. The A/B test in §6.3 provides the latter over all traffic.

Discovery and Advertising Analysis. We next examine the discovery and advertising results in more detail. Table 4(b, c) breaks down DCGR’s comparison with the corresponding specialized channels.

For discovery, DCGR reaches 4.814.81 categories new to the user per reached user, compared with 2.152.15 for the specialized discovery channel, yielding the 2.2×2.2\times gain in Figure 7. More importantly, the difference lies primarily in which users receive these categories rather than in which items are retrieved. DCGR covers 76.0%76.0\% of the discovery channel’s items but only 11.7%11.7\% of its user–category pairs; in the reverse direction, the corresponding coverages are 14.0%14.0\% and 1.2%1.2\%. DCGR also forms 9.4×9.4\times as many user–category pairs per day, and users reached only by DCGR convert 2.8×2.8\times as efficiently as those reached only by the discovery channel. The two retrievers therefore draw on substantially overlapping items but expose them to very different users.

For advertising, DCGR also takes on a substantially larger role in sponsored-item retrieval. Sponsored items account for 33.7%33.7\% of its exposures, compared with 4.7%4.7\% for the main channel in the control group. On sponsored items, DCGR serves 1.8×1.8\times as many exposures as the specialized advertising channel and achieves 2.1×2.1\times its GPM. This gain comes from stronger downstream conversion and value rather than clicks. DCGR achieves 1.7×1.7\times the orders per exposure, 2.6×2.6\times the conversion rate, and 1.2×1.2\times the average order value, despite a click-through rate about one third lower. Sponsored items retrieved by DCGR are therefore clicked less often but purchased more often and at higher value.

Together, these results show that a single DCGR can cover the objectives represented by zo​cz_{oc}, zd​i​s​cz_{disc}, and za​dz_{ad}, matching or exceeding the corresponding specialized channel on its native metric. This demonstrates the potential to consolidate these retrieval objectives within one model.

7.4 DCGR Decision Dimensions Analysis

The previous subsection shows that a single DCGR retriever can cover multiple specialized objectives. We next ask whether the decision prefix itself carries useful retrieval signals and whether it controls item generation.

Decision Dimensions Carry Retrieval Signal. Figure 8(a) adds one decision dimension at a time to a SID-only GR model and supplies its ground-truth value through teacher forcing. We measure the resulting change in HR@1 across click, cart, order, GMV, discovery, and sponsored-item slices. Because the supplied decision describes the interaction being predicted, this experiment measures the information provided by a correct decision rather than deployable end-to-end retrieval accuracy.

We also discover these dimensions carry different amounts of item information. The purchase level zo​cz_{oc} changes no slice by more than 1%1\%, whereas zd​i​s​cz_{disc} improves all measured slices and za​dz_{ad} produces the largest gains, ranging from 9.6%9.6\% to 20.5%20.5\%. This difference reflects how strongly each decision constrains item identity. For example, za​dz_{ad} restricts a sponsored interaction to the sponsored subset, which accounts for only 28%28\% of interactions, whereas zo​cz_{oc} says relatively little about which item was chosen. The gains also extend beyond the corresponding objective. In particular, za​dz_{ad} improves click, cart, order, and GMV retrieval in addition to sponsored-item retrieval. No measured slice decreases by more than 1%1\%.

Decision Dimensions Control Generation. Teacher forcing shows that a correct decision is informative, but serving relies on decisions predicted by the model. We therefore intervene on one predicted dimension during free-running beam search. If the SID decoder ignored the prefix, forcing a decision would have little effect. Figure 8(b) shows the opposite. Forcing za​dz_{ad} to sponsored raises sponsored-item HR@1 by 31.5%31.5\% and GMV HR@1 by 16.0%16.0\%, while reducing click HR@1 by 19.6%19.6\%. Forcing a multi-order zo​cz_{oc} raises GMV HR@1 by 12.8%12.8\% but reduces click HR@1 by 17.6%17.6\%. Forcing zd​i​s​cz_{disc} toward discovery raises its own slice by 3.1%3.1\%. Changing a decision therefore changes the retrieved items in the expected direction.

The intervention size also depends on how often the forced value already occurs. Sponsored items account for 28%28\% of interactions, whereas interactions in a category new to the user already make up roughly three quarters, leaving fewer requests for discovery forcing to change. The small offline discovery movement also does not contradict its larger online gain in §7.3, nor does the slight drop in click HR@1 under zo​c=0z_{oc}{=}0 contradict its CTR gain online in Table 5. Offline HR@1 rewards reproducing the logged item, whereas online metrics reward exposures that users click or that reach valuable categories new to the user, even when the retrieved item differs from the log.

7.5 DCGR Decision Steering and Prefix Design

We next examine how the decision dimensions should be steered and organized in practice.

Predicted vs. Supplied Decisions. A natural alternative to predicting the decision prefix is to supply the desired decision directly, as objective-conditioned methods do [40]. Table 5 compares this hard conditioning with DCGR’s business offset in an online retrieval-stage A/B test. We either force zo​c=0z_{oc}=0 toward clicks, force za​o​vz_{aov} to its highest value, or apply the offset at increasing strengths. Hard forcing approximates the extreme of objective steering, whereas the offset gradually tilts the model’s predicted distribution.

Hard forcing behaves much like an objective-specific channel. Table 5 shows that forcing zo​c=0z_{oc}=0 raises CTR by 8.2%8.2\% but lowers GMV by 5.1%5.1\%, while forcing the highest za​o​vz_{aov} value raises AOV by 38.9%38.9\% but lowers orders by 33.5%33.5\% and GMV by 7.7%7.7\%. The business offset instead provides a gradual trade-off. As its strength increases from weak to strong, GMV rises from +7.5%+7.5\% to +26.7%+26.7\%, while CTR moves from +2.2%+2.2\% to −5.4%-5.4\%. The offset therefore steers the model toward a business objective without replacing its predicted decision with a fixed value.

Table 6 presents a second retrieval-stage A/B test, which confirms the same trade-off at the system level. Unlike Table 5, it measures all exposures per user rather than only those credited to DCGR. Steering zo​cz_{oc} alone increases orders by 2.4%2.4\% but reduces GMV by 0.6%0.6\%. Adding za​o​vz_{aov} trades some orders for higher AOV, turning the GMV change positive and reaching +3.0%+3.0\% at the stronger setting. The two dimensions therefore control complementary aspects of business value.

Organizing the Decision Prefix. The complementary roles of zo​cz_{oc} and za​o​vz_{aov} motivate modeling purchase quantity and value separately. Replacing them with a single GMV token reduces transaction-value-weighted HR@1 by 9%9\%. A separate purchase indicator is also redundant because zo​c=0z_{oc}=0 already represents a non-converting interaction, and adding one leaves HR@1 unchanged.

Independent decision dimensions should not be chained arbitrarily because chaining requires choosing a decoding order. Table 7 tests this effect on an earlier configuration with three binary dimensions for order, cold-start, and discovery. The order objective performs best when decoded first, and the order-first configurations also achieve the highest weighted HR@128. The decoding order therefore biases which objective is favored. DCGR avoids this bias by combining independent dimensions into the parallel decision token DTp\texttt{DT}^{p} and chaining only genuinely dependent decisions, with za​o​vz_{aov} following zo​cz_{oc} in DTd\texttt{DT}^{d}. This design also shortens the prefix, but its main advantage is avoiding ordering bias, since the summed dimensions share one position and have no decoding order.

7.6 Architecture Analysis

We now analyze the architecture components introduced in §4.3, namely GQA, gated attention, and MoE. Figure 9 reports what gated attention and MoE contribute to OneTrans-V2L on the fine-rank task, and then what each design choice inside the MoE block contributes.

Replacing full multi-head attention with GQA leaves fine-rank quality effectively unchanged, so GQA’s smaller key/value cache costs no accuracy. Figure 9(a) further shows that gated attention contributes 0.08%0.08\% CTR AUC and 0.15%0.15\% CTR UAUC over the conventional attention it replaces.

MoE contributes more than gated attention, gaining 0.13%0.13\% CTR AUC and 0.30%0.30\% CTR UAUC over a compute-matched dense FFN. Figure 9(b) looks inside the MoE block. Fine-grained experts contribute 0.01%0.01\% CTR AUC and 0.04%0.04\% CTR UAUC over fewer, wider experts of the same total parameter count, and the shared expert contributes 0.02%0.02\% and 0.07%0.07\% over the same MoE without a shared expert. The sigmoid router contributes more than either, with 0.10%0.10\% CTR AUC and 0.20%0.20\% CTR UAUC over a softmax router.55 5 Repeated runs of the same configuration differ by about 0.006%0.006\% in CTR AUC and 0.012%0.012\% in CTR UAUC (§7.7), so a difference larger than this should be read as meaningful.

7.7 Stabilization Analysis

We analyze the effectiveness of our stabilization methods introduced in §4.3. Each experiment below removes one technique from OneTrans-V2 and measures how much the same widening of the model gains without and with that technique, each against a narrow model built the same way. The widening gain therefore differs from paragraph to paragraph because the reference differs, so gains are comparable within one figure but not across figures. The gain of widening the full configuration is the one reported for AdamW in Figure 10.

AdamW and Weight Decay. RMSProp [43] is the optimizer commonly used to train industrial recommendation models, and the RMSProp baseline here uses the learning rate, ϵ\epsilon, and decay coefficient tuned for our deployed models. As Figure 10 shows, it yields a large standard deviation across repeated runs, and widening the model brings no gain. We then replace it with Adam [18] under the same learning rate and ϵ\epsilon, with β2\beta_{2} set to the RMSProp decay coefficient and β1=0\beta_{1}{=}0 (§6.1) so that no momentum is added. The only difference between the two optimizers is then the bias correction of the second-moment estimate. This correction prevents the inflated effective learning rate of the early updates. It cuts the standard deviation of CTR AUC from 0.085%0.085\% to 0.006%0.006\% and of CTR UAUC from 0.105%0.105\% to 0.012%0.012\%, both estimated from the same three runs. Widening then becomes effective, turning the negative outcome under RMSProp into a gain of 0.15%0.15\% CTR UAUC. Adding decoupled weight decay on top, i.e., AdamW, raises that gain further to nearly 0.3%0.3\% CTR UAUC while the standard deviation stays at the same low level.

QKNorm. Figure 11(a) shows that widening the model without QKNorm falls short of the expected gain, changing fine-rank by −0.04%-0.04\% CTR AUC and −0.01%-0.01\% CTR UAUC. Once QKNorm is introduced, the same widening gains +0.09%+0.09\% CTR AUC and +0.16%+0.16\% CTR UAUC.

μ\muP. Figure 11(b) shows that widening the model without μ\muP, keeping the hyperparameters tuned at the original width, brings only a slight improvement of +0.03%+0.03\% CTR AUC and +0.07%+0.07\% CTR UAUC. Under standard parameterization these hyperparameters are no longer the right ones once the model is widened, so every widening would call for a new search. μ\muP instead keeps the optimal hyperparameters invariant to width, i.e., hyperparameter transfer [48]. The same widening then yields +0.09%+0.09\% CTR AUC and +0.20%+0.20\% CTR UAUC without any retuning.

Depth-μ\muP. The experiments above widen the model; deepening it is governed by Depth-μ\muP (§4.3), which scales both the residual multiplier and the learning rate by 1/mN1/\sqrt{m_{N}}, and we test it here. Table 8 shows that adding blocks to OneTrans-V2 gains only 0.04%0.04\% CTR AUC and 0.05%0.05\% CTR UAUC on its own, whereas the same deepening under Depth-μ\muP gains 0.08%0.08\% and 0.11%0.11\%. Depth-μ\muP therefore turns additional depth into a larger gain.

7.8 Multimodal Embedding and Model Capacity

We verify the multimodal design of §4.3 by comparing SimTier against the multimodal embedding at two model scales. One is our default OneTrans-V2L; the other is a much smaller variant, OneTrans-V2XS (XS for extra small), which is roughly 46×46\times cheaper to train.

As shown in Figure 12, the two scales call for opposite designs. At the smaller scale, only SimTier helps, contributing 0.07%0.07\% CTR AUC and 0.10%0.10\% CTR UAUC. The multimodal embedding contributes −0.05%-0.05\% and −0.10%-0.10\%, so feeding the embedding directly hurts a model of this size. At the larger scale both ways help, and the multimodal embedding becomes the more valuable choice, contributing 0.21%0.21\% against 0.08%0.08\% CTR AUC and 0.33%0.33\% against 0.14%0.14\% CTR UAUC without any precomputed feature. The multimodal embedding and the model’s own learned item embeddings live in different spaces, and mapping one onto the other is something the model must learn. We hypothesize that a small model lacks the capacity to learn this mapping, so the similarity has to be precomputed for it. OneTrans-V2L learns the mapping on its own and gains more from the multimodal embedding than from a precomputed summary of it. How the multimodal embedding should enter a ranking model is therefore not a fixed design choice but a function of capacity, and a practice established at one scale need not be the best one at the next.

7.9 Training and Inference Speedup

We first analyze the training speedup brought by SNT (§4.4), and then the inference speedup brought by the serving optimizations of §5.2, first those specific to retrieval decoding and then those that apply to the whole model.

Sequence-Native Training. We compare SNT against the exposure-centric samples of Figure 4(a), in which every exposure is a separate sample that encodes its own copy of the behavior sequence. Sharing one encoding across all exposures of a user window yields a 4.4×4.4\times training speedup under the same hardware budget. In these experiments a mini-batch is organized by user windows, each holding the exposures of one user within a window of time. We cut the windows at day boundaries, so that no window straddles an evaluation date and the daily metrics of §6.1 stay comparable with those of the baselines. This choice caps the speedup, since a window can share the sequence encoding only among the exposures of one day. Windows cut by week or by month raise the speedup further, and we leave that configuration to future work. SNT also saves storage. Each user’s behavior sequence is stored once instead of once per exposure, which cuts sequence feature storage by 95%95\%. The exposures of a user are stored next to each other, which makes their non-sequential features compress better and cuts that storage by half.

Retrieval Decoding Optimization. We further analyze the two decoding optimizations on the retrieval task. For SID decoding, Figure 13(a) shows that the two-stage top-kk raises throughput by 19.7×19.7\times under the online latency budget, against our own single-stage implementation rather than the deployed retrieval baseline. Per request, the same change cuts beam-search latency by 2.3×2.3\times. The throughput gain exceeds the latency gain because throughput is measured at the largest batch that fits the latency budget. Shrinking the candidate pool from the beam width times the vocabulary size to kk per beam lets each GPU serve a much larger batch within that budget. Optimizing this step matters because, before this change, 94%94\% of the retrieval task’s inference time was spent in the top-kk. Scoring the decision prefix in a single step then removes the sequential prefix steps, so each remaining step carries a larger batch and maps better onto the GPU. This cuts the measured latency by about 30%30\% against decoding the prefix step by step and raises the cumulative decoding speedup to 27.6×27.6\times.

Overall Serving Optimization. The decoding optimizations above are specific to retrieval, whereas kernel fusion and FP8 serving apply to the whole model. Figure 13(b) measures them on the fine-rank task, relative to the deployed fine-rank model under the same latency budget. Without them the unified model serves at 0.58×0.58\times the throughput of the deployed model, since its fine-rank task spends more compute per request. Kernel fusion raises this to 1.66×1.66\times and FP8 serving to 2.16×2.16\times, so the unified model serves the fine-rank stage 2.16×2.16\times faster than the specialized model it replaces despite its larger compute. Sharing one user context across the three stages (§5.1) encodes the behavior sequence once per request rather than once per stage, which adds a further 1.53×1.53\times on top of all per-stage optimizations, measured over the whole cascade. The two together yield the end-to-end 3.2×3.2\times QPS of §6.3.

8 Conclusion

We present OneTrans-V2, one Transformer that serves retrieval, pre-rank, and fine-rank in an industrial recommendation cascade system. OneTrans-V2 builds on three key ideas. First, it unifies retrieval, pre-rank, and fine-rank within one Transformer model by sharing the candidate-independent user context across stages while preserving each stage’s native candidate features and computation. Second, DCGR consolidates objective-specific retrieval models by representing business objectives as decisions within a single generative process. Third, SNT reorganizes training around each user’s lifelong behavior sequence and amortizes sequence encoding across exposures. Together, these designs unify the cascade across stages and retrieval objectives while making the resulting shared backbone practical to train at production scale. This unification enables computation reuse, joint learning, and in-model knowledge distillation. It also pools previously fragmented capacity into a shared backbone. We scale this backbone with sparse MoE to increase capacity with bounded activated computation, and use μ\muP-style parameterization to stabilize scaling. In a large-scale industrial deployment, OneTrans-V2 improves GMV by 9.74%9.74\% and, together with a co-designed serving stack, delivers 3.2×3.2\times QPS of the cascade it replaces under the same hardware budget. We believe OneTrans-V2 provides a production-scale foundation for the broader transition from model-per-stage recommendation toward a unified one-model recommendation architecture.
